q: How do you create a chart from scratch with helm create and turn the scaffold into something production-ready?
a: Helm create generates a working skeleton with a deployment, service, ingress, service account, horizontal autoscaler, helpers, notes and a test. It is a reasonable start, but I adapt it deliberately. I remove templates I do not need, set sensible image, resources and probe defaults, and replace the sample nginx image settings with the real application's. I check labels follow the recommended Kubernetes label set, selectors are stable, and names use the fullname helper. I add a pod disruption budget, topology spread or anti-affinity options, security context defaults such as non-root and read-only root filesystem, resource requests and limits, and configurable environment variables, volumes and annotations. Values get comments and a schema, and the readme is generated by helm-docs. Config checksums trigger rollouts on config changes, and image tags default to appVersion but allow digests. I add unit tests, a smoke test, chart-testing configuration and a lint step in CI. Finally I set chart version and appVersion, a maintainers and kubeVersion field, and publish to a registry with provenance if required.
f: Which security defaults do you add?
Why allow image digests?
p: Start from helm create, trim unused files, fix names and labels, add PDB, spread, security context, resources and probes, document values with helm-docs and a schema, add checksums, unit and smoke tests, CI lint and publish with proper versions.
tip: Say scaffold, harden, document, test, publish.

q: How do Helm rollbacks work, and what are their limits?
a: Every install or upgrade creates a numbered revision stored in the cluster. Helm rollback takes a release to a specified earlier revision, or the previous one by default, by computing a patch between the current state and that revision's stored manifest and applying it, which itself creates a new revision rather than deleting history. Hooks for rollback run, and flags such as wait, timeout, cleanup-on-fail and force control behaviour. Limits matter. Rollback restores Kubernetes resources, not data, so a database migration applied by an upgrade is not reverted, and an old application version may not work with the new schema unless migrations are backward compatible. Resources that were changed manually are merged under the three-way strategy. CRDs are not rolled back. Persistent volume claims and externally created resources stay. If the history limit pruned old revisions, they are unavailable. Rollback also cannot fix a bad configuration that exists in every revision. In GitOps setups, rolling back with Helm directly creates drift from Git, so the correct path is to revert the commit and let the controller reconcile.
f: Does rollback revert database changes?
Why revert Git in GitOps instead of using helm rollback?
p: Rollback applies a previous revision's manifest as a new revision, running rollback hooks. It does not revert data, migrations, CRDs or manual changes cleanly, depends on retained history, and in GitOps should be done by reverting Git.
tip: Say rollback reverts manifests, not data.

q: What do --atomic, --wait, --timeout and --cleanup-on-fail do in an upgrade?
a: By default, Helm returns once the Kubernetes API has accepted the resources, not when the application is healthy. The wait flag makes Helm poll until pods, deployments, stateful sets, jobs and services are ready, up to the timeout, which defaults to five minutes, so the command's exit status reflects real readiness. The atomic flag implies wait and adds automatic rollback to the previous revision if the upgrade fails or times out, or removes the release entirely in the case of a failed install, leaving the cluster in its last known good state and the pipeline red. The cleanup-on-fail flag deletes new resources that were created during a failed upgrade, preventing leftover objects. Wait for jobs makes Helm also wait for job completion. The timeout should reflect real startup time, including image pulls and migrations, and also bound hooks. These flags make pipelines safer, but atomic rollback can mask the actual error unless logs and events are captured first, and a rollback itself may fail if data changed. I capture pod status and events on failure for debugging.
f: What is the default behaviour without wait?
What does atomic do on a failed install?
p: Wait polls until resources are ready within the timeout, atomic implies wait and rolls back on failure or removes a failed install, and cleanup-on-fail deletes new resources from a failed upgrade. Set realistic timeouts and capture events before rollback.
tip: Say atomic makes failed deploys revert themselves.

q: What does a Helm release in a failed or pending state mean, and how do you recover from pending-upgrade or failed states?
a: A release has a status such as deployed, failed, superseded, uninstalled, pending-install, pending-upgrade or pending-rollback. Pending states appear while an operation is in progress, and if the client is interrupted, for example a CI job killed mid-upgrade, the release can be stuck in pending-upgrade, after which further upgrades fail with an error saying another operation is in progress. Recovery begins with checking helm history and status, and confirming no Helm process is actually still running. A common fix is a rollback to the last deployed revision, which creates a new one and clears the stuck state. If that fails, the stuck release secret can be inspected and the last revision's status label edited or the bad revision's secret deleted with kubectl, a careful manual intervention, after which an upgrade can proceed. A failed release can simply be upgraded again with corrected values, or uninstalled and reinstalled if it is a new install. To prevent this, use atomic and timeouts, avoid cancelling pipelines abruptly, run deployments serialised with concurrency groups, and keep enough history.
f: Why does an interrupted CI job cause pending-upgrade?
How do you manually unstick a release?
p: Pending states mean an operation was interrupted; check history and processes, then helm rollback to the last good revision or, as last resort, fix or delete the stuck revision secret. Prevent with atomic, timeouts and serialised pipelines.
tip: Say rollback first; edit secrets last.

q: How does Helm compute upgrades with the three-way strategic merge, and what happens to manual changes made with kubectl?
a: During upgrade, Helm compares three things: the manifest of the old release, the live state of the objects in the cluster, and the new manifest, and generates a patch. Fields changed between the old and new manifest are applied. Fields changed manually in the live object but not touched by the chart are preserved, which is the improvement over Helm 2's two-way comparison. But if the chart sets a field that was manually changed, the new manifest wins on upgrade, and if a field existed in the old manifest and was removed in the new, it is deleted. This means manual edits outside Helm's knowledge may persist unexpectedly, causing drift between Git and the cluster, or be overwritten without warning. Another consequence is that rollback after manual change behaves unexpectedly. Objects not part of any Helm release are not touched. Adopting existing resources requires labels and annotations for Helm ownership. The practical lesson is to avoid manual changes, use diff before upgrades and let GitOps reconcile continuously, optionally using server-side apply to manage field ownership more precisely.
f: What was wrong with the Helm 2 approach?
How can you see drift before upgrading?
p: Helm patches using old manifest, live state and new manifest, so manual changes to fields the chart does not set persist while chart-set fields are overwritten and removed fields deleted. Avoid manual edits, use helm diff and GitOps, and consider server-side apply.
cmds: kubectl get deploy app -o yaml | diff - rendered.yaml
tip: Say compare old, live and new.

q: How do you adopt existing Kubernetes resources into a Helm release, or move a release between namespaces?
a: Helm refuses to install resources that already exist and are not owned by the release, with an error about missing ownership metadata. To adopt a resource, add the label app.kubernetes.io/managed-by with value Helm and the annotations meta.helm.sh/release-name and meta.helm.sh/release-namespace matching the intended release, using kubectl label and annotate; then an install or upgrade that includes that resource succeeds and takes ownership. Doing this for many resources is scripted, and backups of the objects are taken first. Moving a release between namespaces is not supported directly because releases are namespaced and stored there. The safe approach is to install a new release in the target namespace, migrate data and traffic with care, then uninstall the old one, taking care that persistent volumes and external resources survive, perhaps by retaining volume reclaim policies. Renaming a release has the same constraint. Tools or manual copying of release secrets are risky and unsupported. In production, I plan migrations with maintenance windows, validate in staging and keep rollback paths.
f: Which labels mark Helm ownership?
Why can't a release simply be moved to another namespace?
p: To adopt resources add the managed-by Helm label and the release-name and release-namespace annotations; to move a release, install a new one in the target namespace, migrate data and traffic, then remove the old. Releases are namespaced so direct moves are unsupported.
cmds: kubectl annotate deploy app meta.helm.sh/release-name=app meta.helm.sh/release-namespace=prod
tip: Say label and annotate to adopt.

q: What deployment strategies can you implement with Helm, such as blue-green and canary?
a: Helm itself performs standard Kubernetes updates, so rolling update behaviour comes from the deployment's strategy settings, tuned with max surge, max unavailable, readiness probes and disruption budgets. For blue-green, I install two releases, for example blue and green, each with its own deployment, and a shared service or ingress whose selector or weight switches traffic once the new release passes checks; rollback is switching back, and the old release is removed later. Another form keeps one chart with a colour value and flips the service selector. For canary, I run a second release of the new version with a small replica count behind the same service selector, giving a rough traffic share proportional to replica counts, or better, use an ingress controller's canary annotations, a service mesh or Argo Rollouts, which provide weighted traffic, metric analysis and automated promotion or abort. Argo Rollouts and Flagger integrate with Helm charts by templating a Rollout resource. Database changes need expand-and-contract migrations so both versions work. The choice depends on risk, infrastructure cost and tooling.
f: How can replica counts approximate a canary?
What do Argo Rollouts add?
p: Helm does rolling updates via deployment strategy; blue-green uses two releases and switches service or ingress, canary uses a small second release or weighted ingress, mesh, Argo Rollouts or Flagger for metric-driven promotion. Use backward-compatible migrations.
tip: Say Helm ships; a rollout controller shifts traffic.

q: How do you manage Helm release history and cleanup, and what is --history-max?
a: Each revision is stored as a secret in the release namespace, containing the chart, values and rendered manifest. Without limits, frequently deployed releases accumulate many large secrets, which consume etcd space, slow listing and in extreme cases hit object size limits. The history-max option on upgrade, defaulting to ten, keeps only that number of recent revisions and prunes older ones, which also limits how far back a rollback can go. I choose a value that balances audit and rollback needs against storage, often five to ten, and set it consistently in pipelines. For long-term audit, Git history, pipeline logs and exported release data serve better than keeping hundreds of cluster revisions. Uninstalled releases kept with keep-history show up in listings with the all flag and should be cleaned eventually. Failed or superseded revisions are cleaned by the same pruning. I monitor etcd size and the count of Helm secrets, and avoid putting large files into charts or values, because every revision stores them again, which can make a release exceed secret size limits.
f: What is the default history limit?
Why can large charts break releases?
p: Each revision is a secret, so cap them with --history-max (default 10) to protect etcd and listing speed, balancing rollback depth. Use Git and logs for audit, clean kept history and avoid large embedded files that hit secret size limits.
tip: Say cap revisions; Git is the audit trail.

q: How do you handle database migrations alongside Helm upgrades safely?
a: Migrations are the riskiest part of an upgrade because rollback of Kubernetes objects does not undo schema changes. The safest design is expand and contract: first release adds columns or tables in a backward-compatible way while the old application still works, the application then switches, and a later release removes unused structures. This lets old and new versions run together during rolling updates and makes rollbacks safe. Mechanically, migrations run either as a pre-upgrade hook job, which blocks the upgrade until finished and reports failure clearly but is outside release tracking and runs before new pods exist, or as an init container on each pod, which risks races, or as a separate pipeline step or operator-managed job executed once before the Helm upgrade. Migration tools take locks so only one runs at a time. Jobs need timeouts, retries off or controlled, idempotency, and resource limits. Take a backup or snapshot before risky migrations, test on a copy of production data, and monitor lock times. Never combine a destructive change with the release that stops using the data.
f: What is expand and contract?
Why can init-container migrations be risky?
p: Use expand-and-contract migrations so old and new versions coexist, run them once as a pre-upgrade hook job or a dedicated pipeline step with locks, timeouts and idempotency, back up beforehand and never ship destructive changes together with the code that stops using the data.
cmds:
metadata:
  annotations:
    "helm.sh/hook": pre-upgrade
    "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": before-hook-creation
spec:
  backoffLimit: 0
tip: Say schema changes must be backward compatible.

q: How do you use helm diff and a dry-run to review a change before production?
a: Before upgrading, I want to see exactly what will change. Helm template shows the full rendered manifests, but comparing to the live cluster needs the diff plugin: helm diff upgrade renders the new manifests and compares them with the release's current state, printing additions, removals and changed fields, with options to show only a number of context lines, to suppress secrets' values and to include the three-way merge so manual drift is visible. I run it in the pull request pipeline against the target cluster with read-only credentials and post the output as a comment for reviewers, so changes to values or chart versions are visible as real Kubernetes differences, including surprising side effects such as an image change, selector change or removed resource. Helm upgrade with dry-run and debug validates against the API server without persisting, catching admission errors. For GitOps tools, the equivalent is the diff or preview features. This review step catches mistakes that code review of templates and values alone cannot, because the rendered output depends on defaults and dependencies.
f: What does the diff plugin compare?
Why hide secret values in diff output?
p: helm diff upgrade compares the rendered new manifests with live state, including three-way drift, and is run in pull requests with read-only credentials; dry-run adds server-side validation. Suppress secret values and review image, selector and removed resources.
cmds: helm diff upgrade app ./chart -f values/prod.yaml -n prod --suppress-secrets --context 3
tip: Say review the rendered diff, not just the values.

q: How do you roll back safely when only part of a multi-release application is broken?
a: First I identify which release introduced the problem, using monitoring, deployment annotations and each release's history, to avoid rolling back healthy components. If the services are independent and loosely coupled, I roll back only the faulty release with helm rollback to its last good revision, wait for readiness and verify metrics. If a change spans releases, such as an API contract shared by two services, rollback order matters: the consumer or producer must be reverted so compatibility holds, and backward-compatible interfaces and versioned APIs prevent hard dependencies. Feature flags allow disabling new behaviour without redeploying. In an umbrella chart all components share one release, so rolling back reverts everything, which is a reason to prefer separate releases. Data changes complicate matters, so I check migrations. For GitOps, I revert the offending commit so Git and cluster agree, and pause automated syncs of dependent apps during the incident. Afterwards, a post-incident review improves tests, adds canary stages and updates runbooks, and I record the rollback in the change log and alert history.
f: Why does an umbrella chart complicate partial rollback?
How do feature flags help?
p: Identify the culprit release, roll back only that release with helm rollback, respect compatibility order between dependent services, use feature flags, check data migrations and in GitOps revert the commit. Separate releases make partial rollback possible.
tip: Say separate releases allow surgical rollbacks.
